Why Kuwait generates ET demand

KNPC's Mina Abdullah and Mina Al-Ahmadi refineries plus the giant Al-Zour complex make Kuwait one of the world's largest refining concentrations, and KOC's gathering centres and export infrastructure keep upstream inspection running year-round.

Refinery exchanger bundles are examined with eddy current at every major turnaround — bobbin screening for wall loss across thousands of non-ferrous tubes, with array or rotating probes on the indications that matter.

Cracker and polymer plant exchangers carry large non-ferrous bundles where bobbin eddy current is the only practical way to establish tube condition inside a shutdown window.

Above-ground pipeline facilities — pump and compressor stations — bring exchanger and cooler bundles into eddy current scope alongside the mainline programme.

Condenser and feedwater heater tubing is eddy current's core power-generation work — full-bundle screening each major outage with plugging decisions made tube by tube.

What typically gets examined

In practice that means ET work across Al-Zour, Mina Abdullah and Mina Al-Ahmadi units, KOC gathering centres, crude and product pipelines, and power and water plant equipment — with scope set by the damage mechanisms each asset actually runs, not by a standard menu.

Certification and acceptance in Kuwait

KNPC and KOC standards govern — pre-qualification is formal, ASNT Level II minimum with Level III procedure approval expected, and gate passes and HSE inductions consume real lead time that scheduling has to respect.

Examinations themselves are performed to ASME Section V Article 8 and its tubing appendices, ISO 15548, and ASTM E243 for tube examination. The evidence chain — technician certification current on the day, instrument and reference block calibration, and the procedure revision in force — travels with every report, because that bundle is what an audit actually checks.
